paragraphs: Friend, here's what hit me. Jesus tells the Twelve exactly what's waiting in Jerusalem: condemned, mocked, flogged, crucified, and then raised to life on the third day (Matthew 20:18-19). Right after that, a mother kneels down and asks for the two best seats in the kingdom (Matthew 20:20-21). Jesus is walking toward a cross, and the conversation next to Him is about who gets the good chairs. I think that's the most human moment in the whole chapter, and I say that as somebody who has also been busy with the wrong thing at the wrong time.

Jesus doesn't scold anybody. He says, "You do not know what you are asking," and then He turns the whole thing upside down (Matthew 20:22). The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over people, but He says, "It shall not be this way among you" (Matthew 20:25-26). In His kingdom, greatness isn't measured by who sits closest to the throne. It's measured by who's willing to serve. So the question for you and me is not how high we can climb. It's who we can lift today.

And Jesus doesn't ask us to do anything He hasn't done first. He says the Son of Man "did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). The One with every right to the best seat took the lowest place for us. That's why I keep my ovens ready and my sleeves rolled up. When you serve somebody this week, quietly, with nobody clapping, you're following the best Master there ever was.
